notes.1a: Candidates were generally aware of the triple bond in a nitrogen molecule, but not all went on to say that this was a strong bond or required considerable energy to break it.
notes.1b: This calculation was completed only by the more able candidate, with others missing out terms. Even if all the terms were present, multipliers were often incorrect. The most common errors were omitting the bond energy of N (or doubling it), using just the second ionisation energy of Mg, rather than the sum of the first two, and not multiplying the atomisation and ionisation energies by three. Candidates might have been more successful if they had drawn out the energy diagram for the process.
notes.1i: Most candidates carried out these calculations successfully.
notes.1iii: Most candidates were able to give a correct equation.
notes.1iv: Answers to this part were often too vague to be awarded credit. Some candidates referred to lithium metal or lithium nitride rather than lithium hydroxide in their answers.
notes.2a: This part was generally answered well, although a few candidates gave vague answers to one or both parts and could not be credited. The key point concerning a dynamic equilibrium is that the forward and reverse reactions are proceeding at the same rate.
notes.2i: Most candidates gave a correct expression for K .
notes.2iii: Only a fraction of candidates related the value of K to the fact that the reaction was endothermic.
notes.2c: This question clearly divided candidates, with those who understood pH and were able to deal with calculations involving logs often receiving full credit, whilst those that were less confident receiving very little credit.
notes.3a: Candidates gave mixed answers here, with a surprising number omitting to state the oxidation numbers of the four elements. Even those who did do so often did not relate these to the number of outer/valency electrons lost.
notes.3b: Many candidates did not answer the question here to describe observations. Examiners were expecting answers including the formation of misty fumes, the evolution of heat or some ‘fizzing’. There was also some uncertainty about the product of the reaction or writing a balanced equation. Acceptable products were H PO , HPO and the partially hydrolysed POCl . 3 4 3 3
notes.3i: Lots of candidates gained full credit here, although some unfortunately used a correct empirical formula of PCl to get an incorrect molecular formula of P Cl . 2 3 6
notes.3iii: Most candidates correctly deduced that the oxidation number was +2.
notes.3iv: This proved a trickier question with only more able candidates suggesting a correct structure, which could be obtained by replacing all four Cl atoms in P Cl by OH groups. 2 4
notes.4a: All but the weakest candidates were able to write a correct equation here. Common errors were not balancing the equation or including a nitrogen atom rather than a nitrogen molecule.
notes.4i: Most candidates knew about ‘acid rain’, but a surprisingly large number did not link it to SO when SO would also be capable of producing an acid solution.
notes.4iii: A large number of candidates confused K with K here. Even those who gave the correct p c expression did not always state that the constant had no units.
notes.4c: Although a good number of candidates were able to point out that nitrogen and oxygen were present in air and hence it was the temperature of combustion that was significant, many did not appreciate this point and thought that hydrogen would reduce the amount of NO produced.
notes.4iv: Only the more able candidates evaluated this correctly. The most common error was not to square the (99.8/0.2) expression.
notes.4v: As in question 2(b)(ii) only a fraction of candidates realised that they needed to relate their answer to ∆H for the reaction.
notes.5a: This question caused problems for a significant number of candidates who seemed unable to draw upon knowledge from a range of areas of the organic chemistry syllabus. The reactions of chlorine were poorly remembered, or guessed at, with chlorine sometimes absent as a reagent.
notes.5i: Candidates are still unsure about drawing reaction mechanisms using ‘curly arrows’ and this was once again apparent in this question. Even those who were able to give a correct mechanism often did not write the equation for the formation of NO +.
notes.5iii: Although stronger candidates knew the reagents and conditions for both steps, weaker candidates omitted one or both e.g. not mentioning the need for heat and acid/alkali with KMnO or a ‘halogen carrier’ with Br . 4 2
notes.6i: A good number of candidates managed to identify the reagent and conditions.
notes.6iii: Most candidates were able to describe the results of a positive test.
notes.6iv: As in question 5(a) candidates often seemed unable to draw on knowledge from different areas of organic chemistry.
notes.6b: There were a large number of poor drawings of structures here. Candidates must show the correct atoms bonded in the right sequence. Candidates had most difficulty with the structure of D, whilst often giving correct structures for E and F.
notes.6c: In general, those candidates who scored well in (a)(iv) and (b) scored well here too. The most common error was to repeat structures for compounds H, J and K.
notes.7: It was pleasing to see that the whole of this question was generally well-answered making it one of the higher scoring questions on the paper.
notes.7a: Weaker candidates did not relate the loss of enzyme activity to the structure and bonding in enzymes. Examiners were looking for answers which referred to the breaking of a specific type of bond in the tertiary structure of the enzyme.
notes.7b: Most candidates were able to complete the diagrams although in a few cases impossible substrates were drawn.
notes.7c: Some very good answers were given here suggesting that this area of the syllabus had been well- taught.
notes.7i: Although most candidates drew a correct curve, a few clearly had little idea of the effect of non-competitive inhibitors.
notes.7iii: This again proved difficult for some candidates who confused the effects of competitive and non-competitive inhibitors.
notes.8a: A surprisingly large number of candidates were unable to relate the two physical processes to their application in chromatography giving very vague answers which did not score. The key points were that in partition, components are separated due to their different solubilities, whereas in adsorption, the different attractions of the components to the stationary phase were important.
notes.8b: This was well-answered by well-prepared candidates but a significant number of others seemed to guess at the answer.
notes.8i: Many candidates recognised that the halogen was bromine, but a much smaller proportion referred to the near-identical heights of the M and M+2 peaks in the mass spectrum.
notes.8iii: A pleasing proportion of the candidates used the M and M+1 peak heights to calculate the value of p correctly. Unfortunately not all of these followed the instructions given to calculate
notes.8d: This part was less-well answered with a number of candidates giving ions or radicals rather than stable molecules or giving examples that had M equal to or greater than 30.
notes.9a: This was poorly answered with only about half the candidates receiving full credit. A significant number gave glycine as the monomer, disregarding the need for it to have one functional group.
notes.9b: This was again poorly answered, even though Examiners accepted a range of possible valid answers. Some candidates merely repeated one difference stated the other way round. Examiners did not accept water if it was stated as always being produced in condensation polymerisation, but did so if it was given as an example of a small molecule eliminated in the process.
notes.9i: Most candidates successfully gave water as the answer here.
notes.9iii: Only about half the candidates correctly identified Terylene as a polyester, despite the hint given in the stem of the question.
notes.9d: This question required a clear idea as to the difference between the process of addition polymerisation (involving monomers with identical C=C functional groups, although possibly having different side-chains), which can happen randomly; and that of condensation polymerisation, where the monomers had to join at their different functional groups in specific orientations. Only rarely did a candidate achieve full credit. Even those who correctly argued the random nature of the co- polymerisation of ethene and but-1-ene generally did not refer to Terylene needing alternating monomers in order to undergo condensation polymerisation.
notes.key_messages:
• Many candidates would benefit from an increased familiarity with skeletal formulae.
• Many candidates were still unsure about drawing reaction mechanisms using 'curly arrows'. Increased
practice of using curly arrow notation would be beneficial to many candidates.
• Candidates should be reminded that numeric answers should be given to an appropriate number of
significant figures.
notes.general_comments:
This paper provided candidates of all abilities the opportunity to demonstrate their knowledge and
understanding of a wide range of chemistry. Candidates who were well-prepared for the examination were
able to tackle all of the questions. There was no evidence that candidates had insufficient time to complete
the paper.
